name: Intellect versus instinct/intuition
plain_explanation: Bergson thinks we have two different mental faculties: intellect, which is good at handling solid, separate, unchanging things (like a carver dividing a chicken into pieces), and instinct or intuition, which alone can grasp the continuous flow of living reality from the inside.
precise_definition: Bergson's division of cognitive faculties into intellect (naturally suited to the inorganic solid, producing geometry and logic by 'cutting up' the flux of becoming into discontinuous, spatially separate concepts) and instinct/intuition (disinterested, self-conscious instinct, capable of grasping interpenetrating processes synthetically rather than analytically, and connected to true duration rather than space).
why_it_mattered: It grounds Bergson's condemnation of purely intellectual/scientific/mathematical approaches to reality as a kind of 'dream' or 'somnambulism,' and his call to bring intuition back to greater prominence.
historical_origin: Developed across Bergson's works, especially Creative Evolution.
examples: 'Intuition alone is knowledge at a distance. It has the same relation to intelligence that vision has to touch.'
The image of a funicular railway, with life as the ascending train and matter as the descending train, intellect being mere observation of the descending train
objections: Russell: Bergson's whole condemnation of intellect rests 'entirely upon a personal idiosyncrasy mistaken for a necessity of thought' -- namely his own strong visualizing habit of picturing successions spread out on a line
competing_positions: The traditional view, which Bergson calls 'cinematographic,' that a series of static states can adequately represent continuous change
